issues.issue: The comprehensive plan "shall include all public and private projects and facilities which are required, in the judgment of the commission," so its content depends entirely on the contested Section 1.2(g) definition of "project" and feeds directly into the Section 3.8 approval test. Whether private undertakings must appear in the plan at all is settled only by reading the three provisions together.

Section 13.2 requires an annual program covering "the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine," while Section 3.2(b) states the same duty without the six-year benchmark. The governing period, and whether the commission may vary it at will, comes out only from the pair.

The balancing apportionment among signatory parties must be made "by unanimous vote of the commission," while Section 2.5 provides that no action is taken unless a majority votes in favor and gives each member one vote. The two voting rules for the same body must be reconciled, and nothing says what happens if unanimity fails.

The signatory parties "covenant and agree to include the amounts so apportioned" in their budgets, but only "subject to such review and approval as may be required by their respective budgetary processes." The qualification may leave the covenant with no enforceable content.

Subparagraph 6) confers "all corporate powers essential to the declared objects and purposes of the commission," a catch-all appended to five enumerated auxiliary powers. Whether it adds anything beyond the enumeration, and what "essential" measures, is contestable.

The hearing and filing requirements apply to every rule "other than one which deals solely with the internal management of the commission," a category that is nowhere defined and that the commission itself would classify. Rules of mixed character fall on neither side of the line.

The in-lieu payment clause is ambiguous in its grammar: "annual amounts which shall equal the taxes lawfully assessed ... for the tax year next prior to its acquisition by the commission for a period of ten years" leaves unclear whether the ten years qualifies the payment obligation or the measuring tax year. The following sentence's review "at the end of ten years" assumes the former without saying so.

"All meetings of the commission shall be open to the public" admits of no exception, yet Section 14.2(a) contemplates rules dealing "solely with the internal management of the commission" and Section 14.5(a) contemplates personnel decisions. Whether any deliberation may be closed is unaddressed.

The section requires hearings "in all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing," while Section 4.4 independently requires a hearing on each proposed Article 4 project and Section 3.7 requires "public notice and hearing." Whether the ten-day posted-notice regime governs all of those is only answerable across the provisions.

The executive director is appointed and removable "by the affirmative vote of a majority of the full membership," while Section 2.5 requires only that "a majority of the membership" vote in favor of any commission action. The deliberate difference in wording raises the question whether two different quorums operate.

"Financially interested, either directly or indirectly, in any contract, sale, purchase, lease or transfer" has no de minimis threshold or definition of indirect interest, though the commissioners are sitting Governors whose states contract with the commission. What counts as a disqualifying indirect interest is unmarked.

The forfeiture sanction reaches only "any officer or employee," although Section 14.8(a) imposes the prohibitions on "no commissioner, officer or employee." The omission of commissioners invites an expressio unius reading that they are subject to the prohibition but not the sanction.

"Any contract or agreement knowingly made in contravention of this section is void" does not say whose knowledge counts — the commissioner's, the commission's or the counterparty's. The consequences for an innocent third party contractor are therefore unsettled.

Contracts must be let to "the lowest responsible bidder," a term nowhere defined, and the five listed grounds for waiving competitive bids close with "services ... of a specialized or professional nature" rather than a general catch-all. Both the responsibility standard and the exclusivity of the waiver list are open to argument.
The audit must be made "as soon as practical after the closing of the fiscal year," a deadline with no outer limit and no consequence for delay. Nothing else in Article 14 supplies a date.

Each signatory's unrestricted right to examine "all" books and property "at any time" sits against Section 15.1(m), which withholds federal agency status from the commission, and against Section 14.11(c)'s separate GAO audit regime. Which access rights govern federal examiners is not stated in one place.

Subjecting the commission's financial transactions to audit by the General Accounting Office under the Comptroller General's rules is hard to square with Section 15.1(m)'s provision that the commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency," and with Section 2.1's characterization of it as an instrumentality of all signatory parties. The extent of federal audit control depends on reconciling them.

The clause reads "refuse to give all require assistance," an evident grammatical error for "all required assistance," leaving the scope of the duty whose breach forfeits office uncertain. It also makes forfeiture automatic without any finding procedure, unlike Section 14.5(b).

Loans from a signatory party "shall be repaid by the commission through the issuance of bonds or out of other income," while Section 12.1 makes all bonds payable solely from commission properties and revenues and Section 12.3 bars imposing bond obligations on signatory parties. The repayment promise's security must be read against those limits.

The condemnation power excludes "property of a signatory party and any property held, constructed, operated or maintained in connection with a diversion authorized by a United States Supreme Court decree," but the sentence's structure leaves unclear whether the second exclusion is qualified by the first or stands alone. The scope of the decree-related exclusion is the operative uncertainty.

Political subdivisions are "authorized and empowered ... to grant and convey to the commission, upon the commission's request," leaving it unclear whether the conveyance is permissive or compelled by the request. The words carry both readings.

The commission's share of relocation cost "shall not in any event exceed the expenditure required to serve the public convenience and necessity," a cap with no method of computation and using a term of art borrowed from utility regulation. Who determines that amount is not stated.

The blanket permission to occupy streets and highways is made "subject to such reasonable conditions as the highway department of the signatory party may require," with no standard of reasonableness and no mechanism for resolving a dispute. The grant and the state veto are stated together without priority.

The default penalty applies only "in the absence of such provision" by a signatory state's statute, leaving unclear whether a state statute covering some violations displaces the default for all, and whether a state penalty smaller than $50 ousts the range. "Attempts or conspires to violate any provision of this compact" is also undefined as to the mental element.

Tort liability is measured by the law applicable to "officers, agents and employees of the government of the United States," yet Section 15.1(m) provides that the commission is not to be considered a Federal agency for the purposes of the Federal Tort Claims Act statutes it cites. The two provisions point to opposite results on the commission's tort exposure and procedure.

The disclaimer that nothing affects state riparian rights law is difficult to square with Section 3.3's power to allocate the waters of the basin and Article 10's power to condition or deny withdrawals, both of which necessarily bear on riparian entitlements. Section 14.14(a) likewise authorizes condemnation of "riparian rights."

Amendments require "legislative action of any of the signatory parties concurred in by all of the others," while Section 15.1(q) reserves to Congress the unilateral "right to alter, amend, or repeal this Act" and Section 1.4 recognizes a federal power of unilateral modification. Whether the compact can be changed without unanimity turns on which provision governs.

Section 14.21 provides that invalidity of any provision leaves the remainder unaffected, but Section 15.1(t) provides that if Section 1.4 is held invalid the United States ceases to be a party and bound. The general severability rule and the specific consequence cannot both operate on the same event.

The compact becomes effective "thirty days after the enactment of concurring legislation" by all five parties, while the enacting acts of the United States (Section 15.3), Delaware (§ 1013), New Jersey (15.3), New York (§ 3) and Pennsylvania (Section 4) each state that they "take effect immediately." The date on which obligations attached requires reconciling the two.

The bar on undertaking "any project (as defined in such compact) ... beyond the planning stage" without an Act of Congress cannot be squared as written with Sections 3.6, 4.1 and 13.1, which authorize the commission to construct and operate projects on its own initiative. The carve-out for projects using "State supplied funds only" makes the boundary depend on funding rather than subject matter.

The paragraph forbids the commission to "impose any change for water withdrawals or diversions," where "change" is plainly an error for "charge." The mistake goes to the operative verb of the prohibition.

The reservation cuts back Section 3.7, which grants rate and charge power "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party," yet is itself made applicable only "to the extent not inconsistent with Section 1.4." Which of the three provisions governs a particular charge cannot be told from any one of them.

"The executive powers of the President in the event of a national emergency" are neither defined nor tied to any declaration mechanism, and the paragraph does not say which compact obligations yield to them. Its relation to the commission's own emergency powers in Sections 3.3(a) and 10.4 is unstated.

This reservation provides that the federal member and alternate "shall serve at the pleasure of the President," which contradicts Section 2.2's provision that the commissioner serves "during the term of office of the President." The compact's own endnote records that the two were inconsistent until Congress repealed this paragraph in 1997.

The sentence — "construed as impairing or in any manner affecting the applicability to all Federal funds budgeted and appropriated for use by the commission, or such authority over budgetary and appropriation matters as the President and Congress may have" — omits the object of "the applicability," leaving the saving clause without a stated subject. What law is preserved has to be supplied by the reader.

This reservation preserves federal internal revenue taxation of commission bonds, while Section 12.8 declares those bonds exempt from "all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties" — a class that includes the United States. The two provisions give contradictory answers on federal taxation of the bonds.

The disclaimer of any United States obligation on commission bonds sits against Section 12.20(b), which contemplates bonds delivered to "any duly authorized agency of any of the signatory parties" and sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party." Whether a federal agency guaranty is possible depends on reading the two together.

This reservation makes federal technical services discretionary, expressly "notwithstanding the provisions of Section 11.5," under which each signatory party "pledges itself to provide technical and administrative services to the commission upon request." The pledge and the reservation state opposite obligations for the same party.
